To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

expression level‐dependent differences in synonymous codon usage were confirmed for three bacterial genomes, but the strength of these differences varied between the species, and that these expression level‐dependent codon usage features were related to protein abundance in exponentially growing cells.
the relationship between codon usage features and protein abundance is not absolute, but that there are exceptions to this, and that this relationship is dependent on the species under study.
expression level‐dependent codon usage features can be found in the genomes of three species, and that these can be related to the abundance of the corresponding protein products.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between expression level and synonymous codon usage in prokaryotes and how this can be exploited to improve the prediction of protein expression level from genome data.
‘predictive proteomes’, i.e. the use of genome sequence data to predict protein abundance in cells.
the development of ‘predictive’ proteomics, which is the application of in silico predictions of gene expression levels to improve the analysis of two‐dimension gel electrophoresis data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the expression level‐dependent codon usage features in the three species studied are not a direct reflection of the protein abundance.

the relationship between expression level‐dependent codon usage features and protein abundance data is species‐dependent, but that for some genomes, such as Escherichia and Haemophilis, this relationship seems to be strong enough to allow the prediction of protein abundances in silico.
codon usage features are correlated with protein abundance, and that this correlation is species‐specific and expression level‐dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relationship of codon usage to gene expression level is confirmed, although the strength of the relationship is not as strong as previously assumed.

the relationship between expression level‐dependent codon usage and protein abundance is not absolute and that the expression level of genes can be predicted with varying accuracy depending on species.
, for the species studied here, expression level‐dependent codon usage features are present in the genomes of Escherichiacoli, Bacillus subtlis and Haemophillusinfluenzae.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the assumption of a relationship between codon usage and protein abundance can be confirmed with proteome data, but that this relationship may not always be straightforward.
, although expression level‐dependent codon usage can be used to estimate gene expression level in a species, it is not a perfect proxy for the protein abundance of the encoded protein.
the expression level‐dependent codon usage features in the genomes of E. coli and B.subtilis, and to some extent in H.influenzae, can be related to the abundance of proteins in these cells.
